title: Reno-protective effects of statins among patients with chronic kidney disease in Hong Kong: a target trial emulation

sections.abstract:
Many existing randomised controlled trials lack sufficient power to assess primary kidney outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate whether statin therapy offers a clinically meaningful reno-protective effect in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).

In this retrospective cohort study, electronic health records in Hong Kong were extracted to perform sequential target trial emulation. Eligible adults (aged 18+ years) with CKD who met the indication for statin initiation between Jan 1, 2008 and Dec 31, 2017 were included; those with history of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were excluded. Participants were categorised as statin initiators or non-initiators at each calendar month during inclusion period, where statin initiators were propensity score-matched with non-initiators. Follow-up data were collected for all participants until the occurrence of outcomes, death, loss to follow-up (2 years after last records), or the end of data availability (Dec 31, 2022), whichever occurred first. The hazard ratio (HR) of all-cause mortality, eGFR deterioration (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , ≥30% eGFR decline, and ≥50% eGFR decline) and composite outcomes (all-cause mortality, eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , and ≥50% eGFR decline) was estimated by pooled logistic regression using intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) approach.

1,437,014 eligible person-trials were identified (statin initiators n = 30,907; non-initiators n = 1,406,107), from which 30,892 statin initiators and 108,380 non-initiators were included after propensity-score matching. Relative to non-initiators, significant risk reduction was found among statin initiators in all-cause mortality (HR [95% confidence interval (CI)], ITT: 0.97 [0.95–0.98]; PP: 0.91 [0.88–0.93]), progression to eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (ITT: 0.91 [0.89–0.93]; PP: 0.77 [0.74–0.80]), ≥50% eGFR decline (ITT: 0.95 [0.93–0.98]; PP: 0.89 [0.84–0.93]), and composite outcomes (ITT: 0.96 [0.94–0.97]; PP: 0.90 [0.88–0.92]). Statin therapy initiation was also associated significantly with reduced risk of ≥30% eGFR decline using PP approach (0.94 [0.92–0.96]).

Over a 10-year follow-up period, initiating statin therapy in patients with CKD was associated with a small yet significant decrease in all-cause mortality and a modest reno-protective effect. Future research should aim to clarify the effects of statin intensity, duration, and adherence.

National Natural Science Foundation of China.

Keywords: Chronic kidney disease, Statin, Mortality, Target trial emulation, Intention-to-treat
sections.introduction:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global public health crisis, characterised by a progressive loss of kidney function and a dramatically elevated risk of premature mortality, primarily from cardiovascular events. CKD affects over 10% of the global population. 1 In the United States, CKD affects more than one in seven adults, equating to an estimated 35.5 million individuals. 2 High prevalence rates have also been corroborated by studies in Europe and Asia. 3 , 4 The increasing global burden of CKD is partly attributable to population ageing. The number of individuals undergoing dialysis is also rising worldwide, with particularly rapid increases observed in Asia. 5 This condition imposes a substantial burden on healthcare systems globally. With limited effective treatments available to slow its progression, much of the clinical focus is on managing its severe comorbidities. Chief among these is cardiovascular disease, for which CKD is a potent and independent risk factor.

The risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) increases as kidney function deteriorates, starting from the early stages of CKD. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that statins are beneficial in various stages of CKD in preventing cardiovascular diseases like coronary events, strokes, myocardial infarction and cardiovascular mortality by lowering low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). 6 , 7 , 8 In addition, statins have been proposed to have “pleiotropic effects” which are favourable for reducing CKD progression, such as lowering oxidative stress, reducing inflammation, and stabilising atherosclerotic plaques. 9 However, whether these established cardiovascular benefits and proposed pleiotropic effects translate into a direct, clinically meaningful preservation of kidney function remains a subject of debate and conflicting evidence.

In clinical research, the impact of statins on the decline of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in CKD has yielded inconsistent findings. A large study focusing on hard kidney outcomes, such as the initiation of dialysis or transplantation, kidney failure, mortality, or a doubling of baseline creatinine levels, did not demonstrate a reno-protective effect from the combination of simvastatin and ezetimibe. 8 Conversely, other meta-analyses have linked statin use to reductions in proteinuria, although they indicate only a modest preservation of eGFR at best. 10 , 11

Thus, a critical evidence gap persists regarding the reno-protective efficacy of statins, largely because existing randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have not been adequately powered or designed with primary kidney outcomes in mind. Given the ethical and logistical challenges of conducting a new large-scale RCT for this purpose, we sought to address this gap via a target trial emulation. Therefore, the objective of this study was to emulate a target trial to investigate whether statin therapy has a clinically significant reno-protective effect in patients with CKD. We hypothesised that initiating statin therapy would be associated with a reduced risk of major adverse kidney events compared to non-initiation.
sections.methods:
In this retrospective cohort study, electronic health records in Hong Kong were extracted to perform sequential target trial emulation. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of The University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority Hong Kong West Cluster (reference number UW 19-362). Anonymised data were extracted from clinical management system database, and hence informed consent from patients was not required.

Electronic health records, including demographics, diagnoses, laboratory results, prescriptions and attendance of public healthcare services, were extracted from Hospital Authority's Clinical Management System (HA-CMS). The HA is a statutory administrative organisation that oversees majority of public inpatient and outpatient healthcare services in Hong Kong, China. HA also maintains comprehensive electronic records of patient encounters within the public system, providing real-time data to facilitate clinical management across all clinics and hospitals within the HA. Data on death was retrieved from the Hong Kong Deaths Registry. The Hong Kong Deaths Registry, operated by the Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China, manages records of all registered deaths for residents of Hong Kong, China. These databases have been used in prior studies which evaluated the benefits and safety of statin therapy. 12 , 13 , 14

The baseline month was defined as the calendar month in which all patients met the eligibility criteria for inclusion into the trials. Baseline measurements were identified as the nearest available data within 12 months prior to the baseline month. Indications for statin therapy included: 1) LDL-C level ≥2.6 mmol/L, or 2) diagnosed cardiovascular disease (coronary heart disease, stroke, or heart failure) with LDL-C level ≥1.8 mmol/L.

The study population comprised all adults aged 18 years or older who, in each calendar month between January 2008 and December 2017, met the following criteria: 1) presence of CKD, defined as baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; 2) absence of a history of eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; and 3) fulfilment of the statin therapy indication. Individuals 1) with any prescription record of statins before baseline month, or lipid-lowering drugs on or before baseline month, OR 2) history of cancers were excluded from the study.

Follow-up data were collected for all eligible patients until the occurrence of outcomes, death, loss to follow-up (2 years after the last records to public healthcare utilisation, including primary, secondary, and tertiary care), or the end of data availability (31 December 2022), whichever occurred first.

Statin therapy referred to any prescription of simvastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin, rosuvastatin, lovastatin, pitavastatin, and/or pravastatin. The outcomes of interest included incidence of all-cause mortality, eGFR deterioration (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , ≥30% eGFR decline, and ≥50% eGFR decline), and composite outcomes (all-cause mortality, eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , and ≥50% eGFR decline).

Baseline covariates included socio-demographics, clinical parameters, and clinical characteristics. Socio-demographics comprised gender, age and smoking status. Clinical parameters included LDL-C, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), triglycerides, and eGFR. Clinical characteristics included diagnosis of comorbidity (hypertension, obesity, diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, dementia, and Charlson Comorbidity Index [CCI]), history of prescription within 1 year before baseline (aspirin, insulin, oral antidiabetic drugs, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, and angiotensin-receptor blocker, β-blocker, calcium-channel blockers, diuretics), and healthcare service utilisation 1 year prior to baseline month (specialist out-patient clinic attendance and hospitalisation).

Electronic health records were extracted from HA-CMS to evaluate the association between statin therapy and the risk of eGFR deterioration. Target trial emulation and specification were illustrated in Supplementary Table S1 . By adopting the approach of sequence trial, all eligible patients at each calendar month during the inclusion period were categorised as statin initiators or non-initiators, respectively. The design of sequence trial emulation was detailed in Supplementary Figure S1 . Randomisation of treatment assignment for eligible person-trials was emulated by 1:4 propensity score matching (calliper: 0.2). Propensity score was estimated by performing logistic regression of treatment grouping on year of inclusion and aforementioned baseline covariates. The balance of baseline covariates in the cohort after matching was evaluated with absolute standardised mean difference (ASMD), and ASMD ≤0.1 was considered acceptable. 15

Target trial emulation approach was employed to estimate both intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) effects of statin therapy on all-cause mortality and eGFR deterioration ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

In ITT analysis, statin initiators and non-initiators were classified based on their treatment strategy at baseline and all outcomes were used whether or not they deviated from the treatment strategy. Odds ratios (ORs) were derived using pooled logistic regression models that included a binary indicator of baseline treatment assignment, follow-up month (modelled linearly and quadratically), and baseline covariates mentioned above. The pooled logistic regression approximates hazard ratio (HR) obtained from Cox proportional hazards models, given the rarity of the outcomes on a monthly basis. 16 For the analysis of eGFR deterioration, all-cause mortality was considered as competing event; therefore, time-varying inverse probability weights for not-dying were applied to account for this competing risk in the models.

In PP analysis, we estimated the hypothetical effect of remaining on statin therapy versus never using it. We defined treatment deviations as intercurrent events. These deviations included: (1) discontinuation of statin therapy in the initiator group, or (2) initiation of statin therapy in the non-initiator group. Patients were artificially censored at the time of these deviations unless indication (for non-initiators at baseline) or contraindication (for initiators at baseline) for statin therapy was developed. In this study, the indications for statin initiation were 1) LDL-C ≥ 2.6 mmol/L OR 2) LDL-C ≥ 1.8 mmol/L and with history of CVDs (coronary heart disease, stroke and heart failure). The contraindications for discontinuation of statin therapy were occurrence of adverse events of statin treatment (liver dysfunction and myopathies). Potential bias may be introduced by artificial censoring when patients deviated from assigned treatment groups. Hence, at each calendar month, each person-trial was weighted by inverse probability of remaining in the assigned treatment strategy, conditional on baseline and post-baseline time-varying covariates. 17 , 18 The estimated inverse probability was stabilised with the probability of staying at assigned group adjusted with baseline covariates only. For outcomes related to eGFR deterioration, competing risk for all-cause mortality was also adjusted for in the model. Cumulative stabilised inverse probability weight for each time point was estimated, which refers to the products of each weights from baseline to that time. The weights were further truncated at 5th and 95th percentile to reduce the impacts of extreme weights. 19 The PP effect on statin initiators compared with non-initiators was estimated by fitting pooled logistic regression model with binary variable of assigned treatment groups at baseline, month of follow-up (linear and quadratic term) and aforementioned baseline covariates. Truncated stabilised weights were also applied to the model.

Absolute risk for incidence of outcomes was estimated by fitting the pooled logistic model with additional interaction term between assigned treatment group and month of follow-up (linear and quadratic terms). The 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the absolute risk were estimated from bootstrapping of 100 samples. All statistical tests were conducted with R software version 4.2.1. All tests were two-tailed and p < 0.05 was defined as statistically significant.

The ITT and PP effect of statin therapy on the outcomes were estimated for subsets of person-trials after stratification into subgroups, including gender (male, female), age (<65, ≥65 years), CCI (<6, ≥6), eGFR (≤30, >30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), and LDL-C levels (≤2.6, >2.6 mmol/L) at baseline. To formally assess whether the treatment effect varied across these subgroups, interaction terms were added into the regression models. The statistical significance of the interaction term was evaluated to determine if the treatment effect was heterogeneous between the subgroups.

Four sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of main results. First, competing risk with all-cause mortality was not adjusted for in the pooled logistic regression model. Second, 1:10 propensity score matching was performed for patient inclusion. Third, person-trials with two occurrences of eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 within 3 months were defined as patients with CKD. Lastly, the person-trials with two occurrences of eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 across period of at least 3 months were defined as patients with CKD.

The funder did not have any role in study design; data collection, analysis, and interpretation; report writing; nor the decisions to submit this manuscript for publication.
sections.results:
Between January 2008 and December 2017, 1,437,014 eligible person-trials (Statin initiator: 30,907; Non-initiator: 1,406,107) with CKD were identified from 120 trials. After 1:4 propensity score matching, 30,892 initiators were matched with 108,380 non-initiators ( Fig. 1 ).

Flowchart of patient inclusion . LDL-C = low-density lipoprotein cholesterol; eGFR = estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate; CVD = Cardiovascular disease. ∗ Baseline measurements defined as the nearest measurement within 1 year prior to the month of inclusion into the study. ∗∗ Indications of using statin include: 1. LDL-C level ≥2.6 mmol/L or 2. with diagnosed CVDs (coronary heart disease, stroke or heart failure) and LDL-C level ≥1.8 mmol/L. § The factors for propensity-score matching include year of inclusion, gender, age, smoking status, LDL-C, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglyceride, eGFR, Charlson Comorbidity Index, medical history (hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, dementia, prescription record (Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and angiotensin receptor blocker, β-blocker, calcium channel blocker, diuretic, oral diabetic drugs, insulin, long-term usage of aspirin), and healthcare service utilisation (specialist outpatient clinics, and hospitalisation).

The baseline characteristics of statin initiators and non-initiators before and after matching were displayed in Supplementary Table S2 and Table 1 , respectively. The mean (Standard Deviation [SD]) age was 74.02 (12.19) years among initiators and 74.40 (12.93) years among non-initiators. The mean (SD) eGFR was 45.86 (10.85) mL/min/1.73 m 2 for initiators and 46.00 (10.69) mL/min/1.73 m 2 for non-initiators. The mean (SD) LDL-C levels were 3.65 (1.00) mmol/L and 3.54 (0.95) mmol/L for initiators and non-initiators, respectively. Despite slight imbalance observed for LDL-C at baseline (ASMD: 0.12), all other baseline characteristics were well balanced with ASMD below 0.1.

Baseline characteristics of eligible person-trials after one-to-four propensity score matching.

SD = Standard deviation; ASMD = Absolute standardised mean difference; LDL-C = Low density lipoprotein–cholesterol; HDL-C = High density lipoprotein-cholesterol; eGFR = estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate; COPD = Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; ACEI/ARB = Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and angiotensin receptor blocker; SOPC = Specialist out-patient clinics.

ASMD ≤0.1 indicates balance between groups.

Prescription and use of service utilisation was measured within 12 months before baseline month.

Fig. 2 presented the estimated HR for eGFR deterioration and all-cause mortality in ITT and PP approaches. Under ITT approach, as compared with non-initiators, statin initiators associated significantly with reduced risk of all-cause mortality (HR: 0.97 [95% CI 0.95–0.98]), eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (HR: 0.91 [95% CI 0.89–0.93]), eGFR ≥50% decline (HR: 0.95 [95% CI 0.93–0.98]), and composite outcomes (HR: 0.96 [95% CI 0.94–0.97]) ( Fig. 2 ) Under PP approach, statin initiators associated significantly with reduced risk of all outcomes of interest relative to non-initiators, which included all-cause mortality (HR: 0.91 [95% CI 0.88–0.93]), eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (HR: 0.77 [95% CI 0.74–0.80]), eGFR ≥30% decline (HR: 0.94 [95% CI 0.92–0.96]), eGFR ≥50% decline (HR: 0.89 [95% CI 0.84–0.93]), and composite outcomes (HR: 0.90 [95% CI 0.88–0.92]) ( Fig. 2 ).

Estimated hazard ratio [95% Confidence Interval (CI)] for outcome of interest between statin initiators and non-initiators in patients with chronic kidney diseases . CI = Confidence interval; IR = Incidence rate; HR = Hazard ratio; PY = Person-years; eGFR = estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate. Analysis adjusted for gender, age, smoking status, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglyceride, eGFR, Charlson Comorbidity Index, medical history (hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, dementia, prescription record (Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and angiotensin receptor blocker, β-blocker, calcium channel blocker, diuretic, oral diabetic drugs, insulin, long-term usage of aspirin), and healthcare service utilisation (specialist outpatient clinics, and hospitalisation), month of follow-up and its squared term. Composite outcomes included all-cause mortality, eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and eGFR ≥ 50% decline.

Fig. 3 displayed the standardised cumulative incidence curve and 10-year risk differences for all outcome of interest in both ITT and PP approaches. Under ITT approach, risk reduction in all-cause mortality (10-year standardised absolute risk reduction [ARR]: −2.2% [95% CI −2.6% to −1.8%]), eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (ARR: −3.3% [95% CI −4.0% to −2.7%]), eGFR ≥30% decline (ARR: −1.9% [95% CI −2.6% to −1.3%]), eGFR ≥50% decline (ARR: −2.4% [95% CI −3.2% to −1.7%]), and composite outcomes (ARR: −2.7% [95% CI −3.1% to −2.3%]) was found in statin-initiators as compared with statin non-initiators ( Fig. 3 ). With PP approach, statin initiators associated with risk reduction in all-cause mortality (10-year standardised absolute risk reduction [ARR]: −5.1% [95% CI −6.1% to −4.0%]), eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (ARR: −11.0% [95% CI −12.4% to −9.7%]), eGFR ≥30% decline (ARR: −6.8% [95% CI −8.0% to −5.5%]), eGFR ≥50% decline (ARR: −6.6% [95% CI −8.3% to −4.8%]), and composite outcomes (ARR: −6.3% [95% CI −7.3% to −5.3%]) relative to non-initiators ( Fig. 3 ).

Standardised cumulative incidence curve and 10-year risk differences for outcome of interest in intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses . CI = Confidence interval; eGFR= estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate. Composite outcomes included all-cause mortality, eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and eGFR ≥ 50% decline.

The findings across all subgroups were consistent with main results ( Fig. 4 ). However, there were statistically significant p-values for interaction in both the intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses, with notable effect modification observed particularly by baseline LDL-C, baseline eGFR, and age ( Supplementary Table S3 ). Similar results were also found in all sensitivity analyses, regardless of analysis approach ( Supplementary Table S4 ).

Subgroup analysis for outcome of interest between statin initiators and non-initiators in patients with chronic kidney disease . CI = Confidence interval; eGFR = estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate.
sections.discussion:
In this target trial emulation, we demonstrated that the initiation of statin therapy, as opposed to non-initiation, is associated with a reduction in the 10-year cumulative incidence of adverse renal outcomes among patients with Stage 3–4 CKD. Specifically, we observed an approximate 2% reduction in the risk of all-cause mortality, a 2% reduction in the decline of eGFR by ≥ 50%, and a 3% reduction in the incidence of new-onset kidney failure among patients with Stage 3–4 CKD. The results from PP, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were consistent with the ITT findings. Our study provides further insight into the small but significant benefits of statin usage in this patient population.

Statins have been recognised for their cholesterol-independent or “pleiotropic effects”. The proposed mechanisms include the enhancement of endothelial function, stabilisation of atherosclerotic plaques, reduction of oxidative stress and inflammation, and inhibition of the thrombogenic response. 9 Notably, statins have been demonstrated to downregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor-alpha, which may mitigate kidney damage resulting from chronic inflammation and reduce kidney fibrosis, as evidenced in in vitro or animal studies. 20

Despite the proposed mechanisms, the reno-protective effects of statin treatment remain inconclusive. The majority of studies focus on changes in eGFR. For example, a meta-analysis of 47 RCTs reported that statins slowed the decline in eGFR by 0.41 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 annually (95% CI: 0.11–0.70) among patients taking statins, irrespective of baseline CKD status. 21 Similarly, Esmeijer et al. included 30 RCTs and reported comparable findings. 22 However, neither study accounted for baseline CKD status. A more recent meta-analysis of 21 RCTs examined the effect of statins on eGFR among patients with, revealing that statin use was associated with only an insignificant change in eGFR (0.38; 95% CI: −0.04 to 0.79). 11 This suggests that the impact on eGFR is modest. Our study, however, prioritised kidney failure events over the annual change in eGFR, as the former is more clinically relevant, and eGFR decline may not always be linear. Our findings supplement previous analyses, indicating that statins are likely beneficial in slowing CKD progression among patients with Stage 3–4 CKD.

A key finding of our study is the modest beneficial effect of statins on CKD progression, which appears to conflict with the results of the landmark Study of Heart and Renal Protection (SHARP) trial. 8 This discrepancy is best explained by a critical difference in our study populations. SHARP was a primary prevention trial, enrolling patients with CKD with no evidence of established CVD. In contrast, our target trial emulation included patients with and without established CVD. Patients with both CKD and established CVD represent a distinct, higher-risk phenotype. They not only share common risk factors but are also in the advanced stages of the “cardio-renal syndrome”, where systemic atherosclerotic burden is a major driver of both cardiac and renal decline. 23 It is plausible that the reno-protective benefit of statins is most pronounced in this high-risk secondary prevention cohort. The higher absolute rate of CKD progression in this population provides greater statistical power to observe a modest treatment effect that may have been obscured in the lower-risk, primary prevention SHARP cohort. This distinction has important implications for clinical practice and the interpretation of current guidelines, which generally do not recommend statins for the primary purpose of slowing CKD progression. The observed reno–protection may be a secondary benefit concentrated in patients with established CVD, the population for whom statins are already unequivocally indicated for cardiovascular protection. Therefore, our results reinforce the critical importance of statin therapy in patients with concomitant CKD and CVD, as the benefits may extend beyond cardiovascular risk reduction to include a modest but clinically meaningful attenuation of kidney disease progression.

Interpreting our findings requires acknowledging the heterogeneity of statin therapy itself. As prior studies have noted, the effects on kidney function can differ by statin type and intensity. 22 , 24 Our study was designed to evaluate the pragmatic “class effect” of initiating any statin, which reflects real-world clinical decision-making. While this approach may mask larger benefits from high-intensity therapies, it provides a crucial baseline estimate of the overall reno-protective benefit afforded by general statin use in this population. Our study bridges the current research gap by taking statins as a whole to see their reno-protective effects as a class effect. From a clinical perspective, our findings reinforce the central role of statins in managing patients with Stage 3–4 CKD. The observed 2% reduction in all-cause mortality aligns with the primary indication for statins—cardiovascular risk reduction. The additional 3% reduction in the risk of significant eGFR decline or kidney failure, while modest, represents a meaningful benefit in a population with few therapeutic options to slow disease progression. Therefore, our results lend further weight to guideline recommendations for broad statin use in patients with CKD, not only for cardiovascular protection but also for a potential, direct reno-protective effect.

One of our study's notable strengths is its use of a target trial emulation framework. This approach enables the precise definition of the causal question and the estimation of intervention effects in an observational setting. Furthermore, one of the challenges with the traditional cohort study is the difficulty in aligning the index date of statin initiators and non-initiators. The sequential nested trial also helps reduce immortal time and selection bias. We also used laboratory parameters to determine the CKD stages and outcomes, rather than relying on diagnostic codes.

Our study has some limitations. First, the lack of information on statin dosage prevented the classification of statin usage into high-, moderate-, or low-intensity. Prior studies have shown a significantly lower prescription prevalence of high-intensity statin therapy in Hong Kong, China as compared to low- and moderate-intensity statin therapy, 25 and a more significant LDL-reduction had a more significantly renal protection compared with controls. 10 , 26 We may, therefore, underestimate the true reno-protective effects of high-intensity statins in this work. Second, it is also worth noting that in our PP analysis, we considered the continuity of statin prescriptions but not medication adherence. Nevertheless, previous retrospective studies in Hong Kong, China have shown that Chinese patients generally exhibit much better adherence with lipid-lowering agents than American patients. 27 , 28 Third, we only consider eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 as kidney failure, without considering the initiation of dialysis. However, such misclassification bias should be minimal as most patients with CKD started dialysis when their eGFR fell below 10 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . 29 Fourth, the observational nature of our study induces restrictions due to unmeasured confounding and missingness on covariates and outcomes. Important information, such as lifestyle and family history associated with kidney outcomes, is not available in the dataset. 30 The risk of missingness on outcomes is minimised with the use of diagnostics codes and laboratory parameters. Further expanding the scope of the current database by including more detailed patient information in future studies should be explored to strengthen the causal inference of the reno-protective effect of statins. Fifth, smoking status was ascertained from self-reported data documented in the electronic health record. The observed prevalence of smoking in our cohort was substantially lower than the 9.9% reported for the Hong Kong general population in the 2023 Thematic Household Survey. 31 However, this misclassification is likely to be non-differential and typically bias the adjusted risk estimate towards the null. 32 Sixth, the observed statin initiation rate in our study may appear conservative compared to prescribing patterns in other healthcare systems. During the study period, statins were listed as a “special drug” within the HA formulary, which mandated specific clinical criteria for prescription. This policy, which was not lifted until 2023, likely resulted in a more reserved statin initiation rate. While this reflects the real-world clinical practice in Hong Kong, China at the time, it is important for generalisability, as the absolute benefits of statin therapy may be greater in settings with more liberal prescribing. Finally, the lack of blinding and knowledge of treatment assignment is another intrinsic pitfall for this target trial emulation. However, eGFR decline is unlikely to be affected by the lack of blinding.

In conclusion, initiating statin therapy is associated with a small but significant reduction in all-cause mortality and a modest reno-protective effect in patients with Stage 3–4 CKD over a 10-year period. These findings support the broader use of statins in patients with CKD for both cardiovascular protection and potential direct reno-protective benefits.
